lines.text: Then here's the map, and I'll be honest about my own seat at this table. That clause buys your silence and your files - it's standard, and it isn't evil; it's how documentaries get made. The question is what the silence costs. Sign, and your quarry story belongs to the show: editors, music, reenactments, a million viewers. Stay local, and you keep the files, the telling, and the right to be wrong in public - and nobody watches. Both are honest choices. What isn't honest is signing for money you don't need and losing files you can't replace. So counter them: license the story, keep the originals. Any producer worth his contract says yes. The ones who say no just told you what your footage is really worth.

lines.text: Full disclosure includes my own institutional interest. The clause acquires silence and files - industry standard, not predatory; it enables documentary production. The operative variable is the cost of silence. Execution transfers narrative control: editors, scoring, dramatization, mass distribution. Local retention preserves files, narration rights, and public fallibility - without audience. Both positions are defensible; signing for unnecessary capital while forfeiting irreplaceable files is not. Recommended counter-offer: license the narrative, retain the originals. A legitimate producer accepts; refusal prices your footage honestly.

lines.text: Then they wanted the silence, not the story - and you just found that out for the price of a phone call. Here's what nobody tells you about the big deals: half the people who sell their stories end up hating the finished show. Their three minutes become somebody else's cliffhanger. The money's real, and so is watching your own night set to scary violins. I'm not telling you don't sign - I'm telling you know what you're selling. A story on this line reaches one county and stays yours. A story on a streamer reaches the world and belongs to them. One of those is a sale. The other is a lease on your own memory.
